* **The Ajuran Empire never sent or expelled people to the Mekong region, nor did it have any administrative or cultural ties to Laos or Thailand.** Historical sources (such as the Ajuran Sultanate Wikipedia entry, 17th‑century travel accounts, and archaeological evidence) consistently locate the empire in the Horn of Africa, and there is no mention of the empire’s “independence” people being linked to Southeast Asia.

Because of this geographic and temporal separation, the notion that the same people who were “declared independent” by the Ajuran Empire were subsequently expelled from a natural boundary between Thailand and Laos simply does not have a basis in any surviving history. The **Ajuran Sultanate** ([Somali]: _Saldanadda Ajuuraan_, [Arabic]: سلطنة الأجورانية), natively referred to as **Ajuuraan**,[[3]] and often simply **Ajuran** or **Ajur**,[[4]] was a [Muslim][empire] in the [Horn of Africa] that thrived from the [late medieval] and [early modern] period.[[5]] Founded by [Somali][Sultans][[6]][[7]] its rise to prominence began during the [13th] and [14th] centuries and by the 15th century, it was [Africa]'s only '[hydraulic empire]'.[[8]] Through a strong centralized administration and an aggressive military stance towards invaders, the Ajuran Empire successfully resisted [Oromo invasions] from the west and fought against [Portuguese incursions] from the east.[[9]][[3]][[10]]

The Ajuran were among the great centres of commerce in the contemporary African and Islamic world.[[11]] Trading routes dating from ancient and early medieval periods of [Somali maritime enterprise] were strengthened and re-established, foreign trade and commerce in the coastal provinces flourished with ships sailing to and from kingdoms and empires in the [Near East], [East Asia], and the wider world.[[12]][[13]] The Ajuran are believed to be the first Africans to have contact with [China].[[14]]

## Etymology

[[edit]]

The Ajuran Empire traces its name back to the Arabic word; إيجار (Ījārā), which means to rent or tax, likely related to the tributes paid to the Empire.[[15]]

## History

[[edit]]

[![Image 11]]

Genealogical tree of Somali clans[[16]]

The Ajuran is regarded as a successor to its more influential predecessor, the [Adal Sultanate].[[3]] The precise origins of the Ajuran vary as they are rooted in traditional Somali folklore. It was in the 13th century the Ajuran first appeared and began gaining power. For several centuries they exerted strong political influence on the inland pastoralists, while also embracing coastal trade and infrastructure.[[17]] The sultanate functioned for approximately three centuries.[[9]]
